extracted.intended_audience: public relations professionals, communications teams, and press-release writers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on optimal press-release word counts and associated structural/quality checks, including recommended ranges by release type, journalist attention behavior, and a short quality checklist to maximize pickup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal press release length (400-word sweet spot)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal press release length is 300-500 words, with 400 words as the sweet spot that balances comprehensive information with reader attention spans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ~400 words when you need to balance completeness and brevity; 300-500 is the recommended 'optimal range' for most releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalist reading behavior (research-based)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalist behavior: 68% of journalists prefer releases under 400 words; they spend 5-10 seconds deciding whether to read a release; 70% stop reading after 200 words; the opening (first 200 words) is critical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design releases to accommodate quick decisions—front-load the news and make the first 200 words deliver core value because most journalists will skim and many will stop after ~200 words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short Releases (under 300 words)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate for quick updates, event reminders, simple announcements, personnel changes, or single-fact news. Keep them concise and focused on the single news item.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard Releases (300-500 words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard Releases: 300-500 words — the most common type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use for product launches, new partnerships, award announcements, and research findings where you need to provide context but still be concise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longer Releases (500-800 words)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserved for more complex topics such as mergers/acquisitions, major leadership changes, and in-depth research that require additional detail and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-form Releases (800-1000+ words)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suitable only for substantive materials like data reports, comprehensive industry studies, annual reports, or sustainability/ESG reports where extended exposition is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: 5-Second Rule (initial hook and structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists make initial decision in 5-10 seconds. The release must: hook in headline; confirm value in subhead; deliver core news in first 200 words; make finishing the rest 'worth it'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat headline and subhead as the primary attention grabbers; ensure the first paragraph(s) contain the essential news so a journalist can decide quickly whether to proceed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit length rubric (qualitative judgments by range)
rubrics_metrics.description: Length mapped to appropriateness: Under 200 words = Too brief, lacks substance; 200-300 words = Brief, fine for simple news; 300-500 words = Optimal range; 500-800 words = Justified for complex stories; 800-1000 words = Only for major announcements; Over 1000 words = Probably bloated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this quick-reference scale when deciding whether your release's length fits the news complexity and the likely tolerance of journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Why length matters (effects of appropriate sizing)
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-sized press release: respects journalists' limited time, is easier to absorb and act on, reduces editing burden, increases probability of full reading, and increases probability of pickup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize concise, well-structured releases because they improve the chances a journalist will read, use, and publish the information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality Test (practical checklist for trimming and clarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Checklist: Does the headline + subhead + first paragraph deliver the news? Could a journalist write a story from just first 200 words? Does every paragraph add information not in previous? Could you cut 20% without losing meaning?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these four tests to evaluate whether the release is sufficiently focused and efficient; if answers are 'no' or 'no'/'yes' respectively where appropriate, revise to tighten content and remove redundancy.
